Chipless RFID tags cost less than a cent, enabling mass deployment for low-cost item-level tagging.
Chipless tags can be printed directly on paper or plastic like barcodes.
Typical UWB frequency bands for chipless RFID are 3–10.5 GHz, 22–26.5 GHz, and 60 GHz.
Maximum effective isotropic radiated power (EIRP) allowed is about 10 mW in 2.4–2.48 GHz band and 25 mW in 5.725–5.875 GHz band.
Chipless RFID tags have no ASIC chip, so their signal processing depends entirely on the reader.
Antenna gain and bandwidth are primary factors influencing retransmission chipless RFID tags.
Backscattering chipless RFID tags encode data in antenna-mode RCS, which depends on antenna design and matching.
On-off keying (OOK) is used for data encoding by presence or absence of resonators or detuning.
Typical read range in laboratory environments is 30–70 cm with 0 dBm transmitter power and 10 dBi antenna gain.
Conjugate matching of antenna impedance maximizes power transfer and enhances antenna-mode RCS.
Structural-mode RCS is independent of antenna load and depends on physical antenna structure.
Antenna-mode RCS depends on radiation pattern and load matching; it vanishes if antenna is conjugate matched.
Crescent-shaped loaded monopole antennas reduce structural-mode RCS without affecting antenna gain.
Data density of spiral resonator chipless tags is about 0.61 bits/cm²; TDR tags have about 0.17 bits/cm².
Radar cross section (RCS) is measured in m² or dB/m² relative to a 1 m² sphere.
Backscattered signal power is much lower than transmitted power and is susceptible to ambient noise.
Chipless RFID tags require large operational bandwidth due to UWB signals.
Antenna effective area can be greater than physical area, indicating antenna efficiency.
The radar range equation relates received power, transmitted power, antenna gains, RCS, and distance.
Backscattering chipless RFID tags act as efficient reflectors rather than radiators.
Chipless RFID tag detection relies on changes in RCS spectral density caused by resonator presence or absence.
